en: The Ninth Chapter. Now, having bypassed the definition of poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*), which was reached according to the order of enumeration but involves much that remains to be said, [the author] speaks of *rīti* (diction):
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ka) Regarding the term "enumeration" (*uddeśa*): the meaning is that since the *alaṅkāra* was enumerated first among the list of "qualities, ornaments, and styles," one would expect to treat it first; however, that order is bypassed.
He states the reason for this bypass: "because there is much to be said.
By this, the maxim of the needle and the kettle (*sūcīkaṭāhanyāya*) is demonstrated.
Locanā:
(lo, a) Now, desiring to define *rīti*, he establishes the connection with the words "Now, as for the enumeration" (*athoddeśa*).
The meaning is that because there is much to be said, [the author] bypasses the sequential order according to the maxim of the needle and the kettle (*sūcīkaṭāhanyāya*).
The arrangement of words (*padasaṃghaṭanā*) is *rīti*, which, like the configuration of the limbs [of a body],
assists the *rasas* and other elements.
— *Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, kha) Regarding the phrase "of rasa and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes all instances where the sequence [of suggestion] is imperceptible (*asaṃlakṣyakrama*).
"Of rasa and so forth" means of those that constitute the very soul of poetry, whose body consists of both word and meaning.
— *Locanā*
The arrangement and composition of words— that is, their specific [structure]—
is manifested through the defining characteristics of particularity;
this refers to *rasa* and the other elements.
Just as a particular configuration of the limbs benefits the self in the world, so it does in poetic compositions.
Furthermore, that [configuration] is of four kinds. (VisSd 9.1)
Furthermore, there are the Vaidarbhī, Gauḍī, Pāñcālī, and Lāṭikā styles;
this is the *sarīti*. Among them—
The composition, consisting of letters that manifest sweetness, is of a graceful nature.
The Vaidarbha style is held to be characterized by the absence of compounds or the use of very few compounds,
as in the verse beginning with "anaṅgamaṅgalabhuvaḥ" and so forth. Rudraṭa, however, says:
The Vaidarbha style is characterized by the absence of compounds or the presence of only a single compound, is endowed with the ten poetic excellences (*guṇa*),
abounds in consonants from the second class of letters, consists mostly of short-vowel syllables, and is easy to compose.
Herein, the ten qualities such as *śleṣa* (cohesion) and so forth, as stated in that [same] treatise, are presented.
*Vijñapriyā*:
The passage beginning with "the auspicious ground for the limbs of the bodiless one" (*anaṅgamaṅgalabhuva*) has been explained.
It consists of compounds of a single word rather than long compounds of multiple words;
it contains syllables with few breaths (*prāṇa*) that are articulated with slight effort, such as *ka*, *ha*, and so forth;
and it possesses the ten qualities beginning with *śleṣa* (cohesion).
Locanā:
(lo, i) Her nature is graceful; her form is delicate.
The mode is the compound.
Herein is the elucidation of the doctrine of the teacher Rudraṭa:
"A single compound" means being joined with a single word or a compound;
"having few breath-requiring syllables" means that its letters are not difficult to pronounce, as in examples such as *mūrddhā*, *mṛdu-vṛtti*, and so forth.
Furthermore, *āḍambara* is a composition of syllables that are brilliant with vitality (*ojas*). (VisSd 9.3)
The Gauḍī style abounds in compounds—
as in the verse beginning with “cañcadbhuja”—
so says Puruṣottama.
“The Gauḍīya style is characterized by the use of many compounds, very long-syllabled words, a dependence on the greatness of alliteration, and few sentences.”
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, gha) "Āḍambara" means composed of exalted colors;
[the phrase] "puruṣottas tu" means "but the Supreme Person."
The previously mentioned "bandha" (poetic structure) is merely a display (*āḍambara*) from the perspective of others;

however, according to this [author's] view, there is the rule that the aforementioned phonemes must be *anuprāsita* (rhymed). This is the distinction, which he expresses by the phrase "dependent on the majesty of *anuprāsa*.
Here, "dependence" (*pāratantrya*) means pervasion (*vyāpti*).
*Astobhavākya* means a sentence devoid of pauses (*yati*). *Locanā* explains:
it is characterized by an abundance of alliteration, being entirely dependent on the majesty of alliteration (*anuprāsa*).
Furthermore, with the remaining syllables, a composition consisting of two [lines] each of five or six feet is considered *pāñcālikā*. VisSd 9.4.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṅa) He states the Pāñcālikā style: "by means of syllables" (*varṇaiḥ*).
This means by means of the remaining syllables that are left over from two [of the other styles].
Regarding the phrase "in all [cases of] the fifth word," here *pada* means *akṣara* (syllable).
Therefore, the meaning is: "in the fifth syllable occurring within a compound.
This applies to both the Vaidarbha and Gauḍa styles.
For example:

"With a sweet voice, by a female bee whose intellect was heightened by the abundance of spring honey awakened by the spring season, and who repeatedly uttered the sounds of intoxication, [the spring] sang out in low, measured syllables."
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ca) "In a sweet manner" means that she was repeatedly sung to by a female bee (*bhramarī*), a honey-gatherer, in a low-voiced way— that is, with guarded syllables, indistinct syllables, and so as to be inaudible.
Of what kind was her sweetness? It was through the very sweetness of her voice;

likewise, she was one whose intellect and wisdom were intensified and illuminated by the abundance and perfection of the nectar—the honey—of the *mādhavī* creeper awakened and stirred by spring (*madhu*); and similarly, she was one possessed by a forest-dweller in rut, for "being in rut" (*unmada*) here refers simply to height.

In this context, the letters *ma* and *na* constitute the fifth syllable within the compound. Bhoja, however, says: "That which consists of five or six combined words and is endowed with *ojas* and *kānti*..."
Poets know the Pāñcālī style to be sweet and delicate.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, cha) Regarding the characteristics of *sampat* (prosperity) produced by the resonance of the throat, Bhoja says: "Bhoja [states] that *ojaḥ* (vigor) and *kānti* (loveliness)..."
The meaning is that it is endowed with *ojas* in the form of intentional depth (*sābhiprāyatva*) and with *kānti* in the form of brilliance (*aujjvalya*).
"Sweet and delicate" (*madhurāṃsukumārām*) means it is possessed of *mādhurya* in the form of distinct word-separation (*pṛthak padatva*) and *saukumārya*.
In the Vaidarbha example, "anaṅgamaṅgalabhuvaḥ," only the fifth vowels (ū, ū, ū) constitute the letters;
therefore, there is no possibility of it being classified as Pāñcālī, which is defined by the presence of all five [vowels] in their entirety.

In the Pāñcālī example, "madhurayā," etc., only the fifth vowels are contained within the compound; therefore, there is no possibility of it being classified as Vaidarbha, which is defined by the presence of the fifth vowel as the head (mūrdhan) of the syllables.

In that context, because of the use of the plural in the phrase "by those suggestive of sweetness" (*mādhuryavyañjakaiḥ*), there is no possibility of its application here [in the example] "by the female bee" (*madhukarāṅganayā*), since only a single letter suggestive of that [sweetness] is present.
Locanā:
*Ojas* (vigour) and *Kānti* (grace) are two specific qualities mentioned in his [Ānandavardhana’s] doctrine.
The Lāṭī style, however, stands between the Vaidarbhī and the Pāñcālī styles.
Locanā:
By the phrase "standing in between," it is indicated that [the Lāṭī] possesses neither too few compounds nor too many compounds.
The same applies elsewhere;
for example:
"This one rises, the breaker of the seal of the lotus-beds—the young *mandāra* flower of the forest-grove on the mountain of sunrise."
"Splitting the darkness—which was like the copper-red interior of the cheeks of an angry monkey, and which tore asunder the kinship of pairs of *kokila* birds distressed by separation."
Vijñapriyā: (vi, ja) "This one is rising"—
in the example from Lāṭa, the blending of both of these will be demonstrated.
The meaning of this is as follows: by implication, the sun rises;
of what nature is it?
It is the breaker of the seal—that is, the contraction—of the lotus ponds, because it causes those flowers to bloom.
Likewise, it has the appearance of fresh mandāra flowers belonging to the forest grove situated on the mountain of sunrise;
it is a dear friend to the pair of cakravāka birds distressed by separation, because it destroys that separation;
and it is as copper-red as the hollows of the cheeks of an angry monkey while it pierces through the darkness.
The redness of the cheek is due to anger, whereas that of the chest is natural;
here, [the words] "breaking" and "Mandāra" [are used].

Regarding the phrase "friend of duality" (*dvandvabandhu*), [the term] "dividing" (*bhindan*) refers to the fact that the fifth class of consonants (nasals) constitute the Vaidarbha style, while the many remaining consonants constitute the Pāñcālī style; thus, there is a blending of both.
Someone has said:
“Delightful due to its soft syllables and compounds, it is not overly abundant with joined consonants (*yukta-varṇa*).
Locanā:
*yuktaiḥ* means "joined" (*saṃyuktaiḥ*).
The Lāṭī [style] consists of the presentation of a subject matter enriched by appropriate epithets.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, jha) Someone says—this refers to the definition of the Lāṭī style.
Regarding the phrase "with soft words" (*mṛdupadā*), the quality of softness applies to both the individual words and the compounds.
"By appropriate conjunct consonants, yet not excessively numerous"—the meaning is that it should be devoid of an excessive number of conjuncts.

"Suitable" (ucitā) means that for such a subject matter, the Lāṭīya style would be one in which the appropriate qualifiers—meaning those free from the aforementioned defects—are fulfilled or maintained; this is the sense.
This also occurs only in the examples already mentioned,
because the phonemes and other elements that manifest those respective qualities have been stated as being employed for the purpose of manifesting those specific qualities.
However, others say:
“The Gauḍī style is characterized by grandiosity; the Vaidarbhī has a graceful sequence [of sounds]; the Pāñcālī exists through a mixture [of these two]; and the Lāṭī consists of soft words.”
In some cases, however, due to the propriety of the speaker and other factors, the composition and so forth are otherwise.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ña) In some cases, even when certain [figures] are not to be employed because of the absence of their respective aesthetic flavors (*rasa*), there may be other arrangements of composition and so forth due to the propriety of the speaker and other factors; thus he says, "in some cases, [due to] the speaker and so forth.
Even in the absence of the manifestation of those qualities, the mere fact of their being composed [in that way] constitutes a different state.
Locanā:

(*lo*, *ṛ*) Although here [in this context] arrangement (*saṅghaṭanā*) and the other [factors] are dependent upon the qualities (*guṇa*), he states a distinction with the words "in some cases" (*kvacit*).
As he has said: "In every respect, arrangement and the rest are based on rasa; however, there is a certain degree of gradation depending on the speaker and other factors."
By the word "vāktra" (mode of address) and so forth, the expressed meaning and the composition are intended; by the word "racanā" (structure) and so forth, the meter and the phonemes are intended.
Among these, an example of appropriateness regarding the mode of address (*vaktraucitya*) is as follows:

"Deep-sounding like the roar of Mount Mandara as it moves through its caverns submerged in the ocean waters churned by the churning-stick, and fierce with the mutual clashing of masses of thunderclouds at the dissolution of the world when struck by the drumstick..."

"By whom has this drum been struck—a drum that is the wind of the portentous thunderclap for the destruction of the Kuru clan, driven by the storm-cloud of Kṛṣṇa’s wrath, and which acts as a companion to the echo of our own lion-roars?"
In this case, although the expressed meaning does not manifest anger and so forth, the composition and other elements are exalted by virtue of Bhīmasena being the speaker.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ṭa) "Manthāyasta" and so forth—this is Bhīma’s inquiry after hearing the sound of the kettledrum on the battlefield:
"By whom was this kettledrum struck?"—that is, produced by the act of striking.
In accordance with the literal sense, the adjectives are construed with the kettledrum.

What is the nature of the sound? It is deep like the roar of the moving Mount Mandara, whose caverns are pervaded by the waters of the ocean that have become exhausted—having undergone fatigue—through churning and stirring; [such is the sound] when there are blows, that is, strikes with the *koṇa*, the striking-stick.
It is the fierce sound produced by the mutual clashing of massing clouds at the time of universal dissolution;
or else, as it is said: "When hundreds of thousands of *ḍhakkā* drums and hundreds upon hundreds of *bherī* kettledrums are sounded all at once, that is called a *koṇāghāta*."

The locative case in "yatra" (wherein) is used in the sense of a cause; thus, the meaning is that among such sounds—such as the beating of a drum (*ḍhakkā*) and so forth—which are struck at a single time, this [sound] is a "thundering" one, and so on, meaning it is fierce (*caṇḍa*). Furthermore, it is the "foremost messenger of Kṛṣṇā's (Draupadī's) anger," because it instigates it, and it is a "destructive wind (*nirghātavāta*)" that portends the destruction of the Kuru clan, serving as a portentous omen.
Regarding the phrase "herein" (*atreha*), the word *vācya* refers here to that which is to be established; thus, the meaning is "of the target [sound], namely the sound of the drum.
Locanā:
In passages such as "churned by the churning-stick," the sentence functions as an indicator of anger, because a drama (*nāṭaka*)—being performative in nature—conveys suffering.

He states the distinction regarding what is inappropriate, even when there is a long compound: the sense is that there is no impropriety in saying "the hero Bhīmasena speaks" [in a manner suited to his character].
Regarding the propriety of the expressed meaning (*vācyaucitya*), as illustrated in the example beginning with "mūrdhavyādhūyamāna... and so forth. — *Locanā*.

In passages such as "mūrddhavyādhūyamāna... and so forth, there is neither propriety of the speaker (*vaktraucitya*) nor, because they occur within a drama (*nāṭaka*), propriety of the composition (*prabandhaucitya*) in the manner previously described;
however, because the poem reveals a haughty subject matter, the diction (*racanā*) is haughty.

Due to the propriety of the composition (*prabandhaucitya*), as in the case of drama (*nāṭaka*) and similar works, long compounds and the like are avoided even when the sentiment is the Furious (*raudra*), because they would be contrary to the performance (*abhinaya*).
Likewise, in the *ākhyāyikā*, even when the sentiment is the Erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), there are no soft-sounding syllables (*masṛṇavarṇa*) and so forth.
In the *kathā*, even when the sentiment is the Furious, the expressions are not excessively bombastic.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṭha) Ākhyāyikā and Kathā are specific types of literary compositions.
Thus ends the commentary on the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Styles" (Rītinirūpaṇa), in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa-ṭīkā* composed by the venerable Maheśvara Nyāyālaṅkāra Bhaṭṭācārya.
In this way, other [categories] should also be understood.
As for Locanā:
(lo, ai), the definitions of the ākhyāyikā and so forth have already been stated.

Since an *ākhyāyikā* is a composition consisting of prose (*gadya*), and since prose is characterized by a rugged style abounding in long compounds, even when treating the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*), a delicate arrangement of words and so forth is generally not employed there.

As the author of the *Dhvanyāloka* has stated: "The propriety inherent in the expression of rasa shines everywhere; however, that [propriety] varies slightly depending on the specific subject matter of the composition."

Thus, although this narrative composition consists of prose, because it is permeated by the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra-rasa*), even when sentiments such as the furious (*raudra*) enter, an excessively florid style of composition and so forth should not be employed.
The same applies to other cases as well.

As stated by the author of the *Dhvani*: "In compositions such as *sandānikā* and the like, because of the propriety of a rugged structure, the arrangement should consist of middling compounds and long metrical feet."
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Determination of Styles" (*rītiviveka*), in the *Locana* commentary on the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*.
Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Determination of Styles," in the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*.
